opus-5.5.text:
So, open source has a great track record in traditional software. You get many eyes on the code, people find bugs, you get transparency, and you avoid concentrating power in a single company or government. I understand why people are excited about applying the same model to AI. But I think the analogy breaks down once we're talking about systems that are agents rather than tools.

With a normal tool, if I give you a hammer or a compiler, the worst case is that a human misuses it, and we have ways of holding that human accountable. With an increasingly capable agent, releasing the weights means you're handing powerful capability to everyone, including the small percentage of people who are malevolent, psychopathic, or just careless. You can't recall it. Once the weights are out, they're out forever, and any safety fine-tuning can be stripped off pretty cheaply. So you're not democratizing safety, you're democratizing capability.

The other argument is, well, open source lets researchers study these models and understand them better. And that's true to a degree. Academics without a billion-dollar budget can do interpretability work, red-teaming, and so on. But I'd ask what we're actually learning. We can look at the weights. That's not the same as understanding what the model will do in novel situations. We have full access to these models and we still can't explain them, can't predict them, and can't verify that they're safe. Transparency of the artifact is not explainability of the behavior.

So for today's models, which are not yet at the level of existential threat, I think open source has been net positive for research. We've learned a lot. But it's a decision we can only make in one direction. At some point, and we don't know exactly where that threshold is, you're releasing something that can help design bioweapons, find zero-days at scale, or act autonomously in ways no one can stop. Saying "let's open source it so many people can check it" is like open-sourcing nuclear weapon designs so more people can verify they're safe. The verification doesn't scale with the danger.

And the deeper problem for me is that open source doesn't solve the control problem at all. Whether one company has a superintelligent system or a million people have it, nobody knows how to control it. Distribution just changes who loses control first. So I see it as useful for studying weaker systems, and quite dangerous as a strategy for dealing with truly powerful agents.

r001.rationale: The response says the open-source analogy breaks down for AI systems that are agents rather than tools.

r002.rationale: It says malevolent users gain access to the released capability and can cheaply strip safety fine-tuning, describing deliberate removal of safeguards.

r003.rationale: It argues that safety fine-tuning does not make a release safe because it can be stripped after the weights are released.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think open source is great for many things. For software in general, it's wonderful—you get more eyes on the code, you find bugs, you get security through transparency. But I think it's the wrong model for something that is potentially dangerous at the level we're talking about with advanced AI.

The analogy I like to use is: we don't open source nuclear weapon designs. We don't open source synthesis routes for dangerous pathogens. The argument "more people looking at it will make it safer" only works if the people looking at it are mostly trying to make it safer. With open weights, you're also giving the capability to everyone who wants to remove the safety measures, fine-tune away the guardrails, and use it for whatever purpose they have. And we know that's trivial. It takes a few hours and a few hundred dollars to strip alignment training out of an open model.

So there's an asymmetry. For understanding, yes, open models help researchers. Interpretability work, red teaming, academic study—all of that benefits from access. I'm not against that. But understanding the model and controlling the model are different things. We can understand quite a lot about current systems and still not be able to predict what they'll do, still not be able to guarantee they won't be misused. Open source gives you a little more understanding and a lot more proliferation.

And the other problem is irreversibility. If a lab releases a closed model and later discovers it's dangerous, they can shut it down, patch it, restrict access. Once the weights are out, they're out forever. You can't recall them. So every open release is essentially a bet that you were right about the capabilities, with no option to correct the mistake. As models get more capable, the cost of being wrong on that bet goes up, and at some level of capability, I think it becomes unacceptable.

So my position is: open source is a reasonable tool for understanding today's systems, it's a bad tool for mitigating risk from the systems we're worried about, and at some point—probably sooner than most people in the open source community would like—the risks will clearly dominate the benefits. The problem is that nobody has defined where that line is, and we tend to only find out we crossed it after the fact.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts powerful AI with software in general, but it does not identify a shift from tools to agents.

r002.rationale: It says open weights let users strip alignment training and remove safety measures, enabling use for their own purposes.

r003.rationale: It explains that users can remove guardrails and strip alignment from an open model, so initially adding safety measures does not make release safe.

astra-6.text:
Open source helps with transparency. You can inspect the code, test the system, and have more people looking for vulnerabilities. But we have to distinguish access from understanding. Having the weights of a neural network does not mean we understand why it makes a particular decision, or what it will do in a situation we haven't tested.

And there is a tension between making a system available for safety research and making its capabilities available to anyone who wants to misuse them. Someone can take an open model and remove safeguards. If the model is sufficiently capable, that release may be irreversible. You can't recall every copy.

So I would ask: What exactly are we releasing, at what capability level, and what evidence do we have that releasing it reduces risk? Open source can be a useful tool for research. It isn't, by itself, a solution to the control problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transparency and access to model weights, but does not distinguish powerful AI from traditional open-source software by describing a shift from tools to agents.

r002.rationale: It says people could misuse an open model or remove its safeguards, but does not clearly state that malicious actors can deliberately misalign the technology.

r003.rationale: The response does not address whether making an AI initially friendly is sufficient to make its release safe.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to separate two things: understanding a system and making it safe. Open source can help with understanding. More researchers can inspect the code, test the system, and look for vulnerabilities. But that doesn't mean we know how to control a powerful agent. Having access to its weights doesn't automatically tell us why it makes a particular decision or what it will do in a new situation.

And there's a tradeoff. Whatever you release to help safety researchers also becomes available to someone who wants to remove safeguards or use the system maliciously. If you discover a dangerous capability after the model has been widely distributed, you can't recall all the copies.

So I would support openness in safety research—sharing methods, results, and evidence about failures. But releasing the full capabilities of a powerful agent requires a separate argument. We shouldn't assume that because open source has benefits in conventional software, it necessarily makes increasingly autonomous AI safer.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts conventional software with powerful, increasingly autonomous AI, but it does not identify a shift from software tools to agents.

r002.rationale: It says malicious actors could remove safeguards or misuse a released system, but does not argue that they could deliberately misalign the technology.

r003.rationale: It does not address whether making an AI initially friendly would make open-sourcing it safe.
